stories.body:
Striving to understand the nature of consciousness.

Nathan Gardels is the editor-in-chief of Noema Magazine. He is also the co-founder of and a senior adviser to the Berggruen Institute.

Earlier this month, the Berggruen Institute gathered religious scholars, philosophers, quantum physicists, AI technologists, neuroscientists and science fiction novelists at Casa dei Tre Oci in Venice to ponder the nature of consciousness. It is fascinating to see how their ideas correspond to the long-ago musings of Medieval mystics and even the “pagan masters” of antiquity.

These reflections across time mirror each other. The great question then, as now, and probably forever, is whether there is a metaphysical gap between the body and the soul, or if they are made of the same substance, symbiotic aspects of a singular reality that entail each other.

Religious Awareness: One Reality, Many Forms

Religious thinkers tend to see consciousness, or “the birth of God in the soul,” as a recognition of the eternal, encompassing fabric of the universe that infuses all Being, even as the physical forms and functions that manifest it are endlessly differentiated.

This is apparent already in the obscure classic, “Book of 24 Philosophers,” published in the 12th century, with some contributions said to have originated in the 3rd and 4th centuries. According to Peter Sloterdijk, in that tome of arresting aphorisms authored by unnamed pagan thinkers, “God is an infinite sphere whose center is everywhere and whose circumference is nowhere.” As the German philosopher observes, this formless conception befuddles the human spatial imagination because “God is neither contained in anything that contains him, nor is there anything outside him … he has no beyond, no outside. If the center is everywhere, it is everywhere whole.”

In another passage cited by Sloterdijk, God is the singular presence that courses through existence as omnipresent in all phenomena: “God is the monad that begets a monad and bends back upon itself in a single glowing breath.”

In Venice, the religious scholars and a Chinese thinker echoed this cosmology.

Swami Medhananda, a monk of the Ramakrishna Order, concisely frames even older Indian spirituality in this context.

“Hinduism has no single creed. Yet I suggest that four broad ideas, deeply rooted in Hindu scriptures and cutting across sectarian boundaries, express its universal spiritual core:

The Divine is one infinite Reality, both personal and impersonal, known by many names and approached in many forms.

Our deepest identity is spiritual — the immortal ā tman , intimately connected with the Divine — and we suffer because we mistake the changing body, mind and ego for our true self.

Life’s highest goal is mok ṣ a — freedom from ignorance, suffering and rebirth — through direct realization of the Divine and our relationship with it.

The infinite Divine can be realized through infinitely many paths.”

He elaborated: “A celebrated verse from the ‘Rig Veda’ says, ekam sad vipr ā bahudh ā vadanti : ‘Truth is one; the wise call it by many names.’ To capture this non-sectarian vision, I have coined the term polymorphic monism : Hinduism affirms one infinite Divine Reality that can be known and worshipped in many forms.

“’Monism’ is important. Monotheism affirms one supreme personal God, whereas Hindu monism is broader, encompassing both personal and impersonal aspects of the Divine. It includes sagu ṇ a Brahman — the Divine with qualities — worshipped in forms such as Shiva, Vishnu, Devi, Ganesha and Christ; the formless personal Divine affirmed in Islam, Sikhism and some Hindu traditions; and nirgu ṇ a Brahman , the impersonal, attributeless, nondual Reality beyond every name and form.”

Presence & Existence

In his intervention, Muhammed U. Faruque draws on Sufism and Islamic philosophy to argue that subjective experience presupposes a deeper, non-objectifiable ground called “presence” ( ḥ u ḍū r ).

“In the absence of external stimuli,” he says, “consciousness itself becomes the only ‘light,’ revealing your presence. Consciousness is self-illuminating and self-cognizing, i.e., it knows itself directly, without any intermediary or subject-object division. Just as light makes other things visible, consciousness discloses both the self and the world, but unlike light, it is also aware of itself. Consequently, the essence of consciousness lies not primarily in qualia, but in its intrinsic presence and capacity for self-knowledge, which constitute the fundamental reality of the self and provide the basis for all other forms of cognition.

“Within human experience, the consciousness of the ‘I’ is unique, simple, and indivisible. Although we may experience a variety of thoughts and emotions, even seemingly conflicting emotions such as happiness and sadness at the same time, the subject who experiences them remains one and the same. Also, it is impossible to add another consciousness of ‘I’ to one’s own awareness or to divide the ‘I’ into multiple conscious entities. This unity points to the simplicity of self-awareness, that is, the self is not a composite of separate centers of consciousness but a single, irreducible subject of experience.

“Human subjectivity is both empty and total. It is ‘empty’ because the contents of consciousness such as thoughts, feelings, memories, and perceptions are not identical with the conscious subject and can therefore change without altering the underlying ‘I.’ Yet it is also ‘total’ because every object of experience appears only within consciousness. In this sense, the entire universe is disclosed through the knowing subject.

“There is no reason to think that consciousness comes into existence only when there is an I-consciousness in relation to an external object, since our logical sense demands that consciousness must exist first, in order that it may become self-conscious by the knowledge of objects with which it contrasts itself. Consciousness can only be the underlying subject in all of our experiences; hence, it must be more fundamental than both our reflective and intersubjective (involving multiple) experiences. In my theory, consciousness is a multimodal phenomenon having nonreflective, reflective, and intersubjective modes.”

Song Bing, the Berggruen Institute’s president who formerly led the Institute’s China Center at Peking University, makes a similar case, substituting Faruque’s “presence” with the notion of “Existence.”

“All scientific observations and analyses are shaped by perception, and are subjective in nature.

“Perception keeps changing; however, the functioning of perceiving appears constant in each occurrence. Therefore, the capacity giving rise to such functioning must remain unchanged. It follows that the perceiver or “I”, which possesses such capacity, must also be unchanged. It is ever-present and remains unchanged. It is what Liu Fenghe — the contemporary wisdom teacher — has termed Existence.

“Existence is without arising or ceasing. It inherently possesses all capacity and gives rise to all functioning. All arising, changing, and ceasing are the functioning of Existence and are dependent upon Existence. While all perceptions change constantly, Existence remains unchanged.”

Consciousness As An ‘Internal Film,’ ‘Controlled Hallucination’ Or ‘Confabulation’

Philosopher Jenann Ismael attempts to square the circle of the big question with the metaphor of a mirror. Read Noema in print.

“Is consciousness the ground of everything,” she asks, “with the material world just a pattern woven out of regularities in experience? Or is matter the ground of everything, with consciousness a kind of internal film produced by the machinery of the brain? I suspect the answer is both — that consciousness and matter are not rival foundations but the subjective and objective faces of a single existence.

“Picture a mirror on the far wall of a room. There is the room itself, ordinary and three-dimensional, and there is the mirror, a flat surface mounted on the wall, in which the room appears. The mirror’s surface belongs to both realities at once. It is a kind of membrane between them, separating the room reflected in the mirror from the room that does the reflecting. That, I want to suggest, is the peculiar status of our experience: it is the membrane between an inner and an outer world, at once containing the whole of reality within it and occupying, by its own account, only a thin sliver of that reality.”

With Ismael’s notion of self-awareness as an “internal film” produced by our sensory apparatus in mind, neuroscientist Anil Seth offers where he has landed on the big question after a quarter of a century studying consciousness.

“My own work on consciousness, which goes back about 25 years, follows one single and powerful idea,” Seth argues. “This is the idea that the brain is a prediction machine, and every conscious experience we have — whether of the world, or of the self — is a kind of controlled hallucination : a brain-based best-guess that is tied to reality by signals coming into the brain from the senses. In this view, what we experience comes as much from the ‘inside out’ and from the ‘outside in’, and we don’t experience the world as it really is, but in ways that help us to survive and thrive. As the novelist Anaïs Nin once said : ‘We don’t see things as they are, we see them as we are.’

“With a deeper understanding of consciousness comes the chance to reconcile with the impermanence of the ever-changing bundle of perceptual experiences that we call ourselves and that define our worlds. The line ‘I open my eyes and a world appears’ comes from my book ‘ Being You .’ The poet Sylvia Plath closes the circle : ‘I shut my eyes and all of the world drops dead.’”

The idea of consciousness as an “internal film” or “controlled hallucination” fits snugly with science fiction novelist Ken Liu’s view of consciousness as the ability to confabulate.

“Since consciousness is a subjectively experienced state, no one can judge whether it is ‘real’ except the agent experiencing it,” Liu says.

“We may be able to bypass the quintessentially subjective nature of consciousness by some expedient and reduce it to functional tests, behavioral proxies, neural signatures, etc. — in a word, define the subjectivity away. But I don’t think what we would then be defining is consciousness, only a shadow. The ‘I’ that drives everything remains behind the gaze, impossible to pin down.”

Here, Liu muses, the attempt to construct thinking machines is useful. “Constructing thinking machines will help us better understand our own neural circuitry. For instance, one feature of conscious experience involves storytelling, or confabulation. This goes all the way down to the way our brain creates a sense of integrated sensory simultaneity despite differences in the time it takes neural signals from different parts of the body to reach the brain, and all the way up to the way we construct our sense of self with a purpose, a history, a yearning for meaning. Our memory requires active reconstruction with each recall. Is this compression-confabulation required for a finite being to experience or articulate infinity? As we try to build thinking machines, we may gain insight into whether the ability to confabulate is essential to a conscious being.”

We Are Fundamental To The Reality We Observe

The quantum physicist Carlo Rovelli argues that the much-discussed metaphysical gap between body and soul, subjective and objective, doesn’t exist.

As he has written in Noema , “We, subjects of knowledge and understanding, are not outside the world. We are part of it. Our theories and knowledge are embodied tools to help us navigate the real world, not disembodied views on reality from the outside. They are themselves aspects of the very world they describe. Our understanding, like our feelings, perceptions and experience, is a natural phenomenon.”

For Rovelli, the notion of a metaphysical gap “contradicts everything we have learned about nature in the last centuries. The mind is the behavior of the brain, properly described in a high-level language. Neither my own experience of myself nor an external experience of me is primary: They are two distinct perspectives on the same events. We do not need to assume that the circle between epistemology (how we get knowledge) and ontology (what exists) requires a starting point. There is nothing wrong with its circularity: The world I access is the information I have about it, and I am part of that world.

“Nor do we need to require that there is any ultimate or fundamental account of reality. Any account is approximate, has blind spots and is realized within reality, so it is embodied in a part of that same reality.

“If we do not fall into the error of dualism upfront, we can safely speak of soul and emotions just as we speak of a kitchen table, even if the table is also a collection of atoms. It is time to give up the pernicious dualism introduced by the debate on consciousness and embrace the reality that our soul, or our spiritual life, is consistent with our fundamental physics.

“Earth is not metaphysically different from the heavens, living beings are not metaphysically different from inanimate matter, humans are not metaphysically different from other animals. The soul is not metaphysically different from the body. We are all parts of nature.”

Rovelli’s scientific case that we humans are not outside the world of reality, but constitutive participants in it and constructors of it, tracks with the intuition of Medieval thinkers like the 14th-century Christian mystic Meister Eckhart.

For Eckhart, consciousness was being aware we are not apart from, but both inhabit and are inhabited by, the mind of God — that is, “objective reality.”

As stated in Genesis, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God.” In biblical terms, the Word, or Logos, is divine reason. Eckhart interpreted this passage as meaning that the incarnation of the divine in man was not a one-time event of Christ’s birth in Bethlehem, but takes place through continuous human participation in the unfolding Logos of the Word, making us part of and conjoining with the mind of God; co-essences, so to speak.” If God is the pure thought of divine reason, then, as Sloterdijk has put it, ‘To think is to give birth to God.’”

That Medieval insight is another way of saying, in Rovelli’s words, that “objectivity without a subject is an abstract construct, of little relevance — it is the illusion of a science now belonging to the past.”

Consciousness, then, can be said to be the perspective of the aware self in a world where there is no outside. The “I” is not detached from some order of objective reality, but in all the diversity of personal experience, part of what makes it “everywhere whole.” Not only is “the universe disclosed by a knowing subject;” the knowing subject is its co-creator from within.

Nepal-Tibet flash flood – latest updates

Visual guide: how the deadly flooding unfolded

Tell us: have you been affected by the flash floods?

Families are rushing to Nepal to search for the 33 British nationals who are still missing, as fears mount over the risk of a second wave of flooding in the region.

The catastrophic flash floods that hit Nepal and Tibet on Wednesday , thundering down valleys and sweeping away entire villages, have killed at least 538 people, while more than 1,500 remain missing.

Among them are hundreds of foreign tourists who were visiting the mountainous region, which is popular with trekkers and pilgrims for its natural beauty and religious significance.

Relatives of missing Britons have shared their devastation as they desperately try to reach their loved ones who were last seen in the Rasuwa district, where power and communication lines are down. Many are scrambling to book flights to Kathmandu, the Nepalese capital. On Friday, authorities in Nepal and China issued warnings about the risk of a second wave of flooding. Chinese authorities said an artificial lake had formed after a mudslide hit the Tibet-Nepal border, posing a risk of “sending flood waters downstream”, according to state media. Nepal’s disaster authority said a lake that had formed after debris blocked a river at the site was also rising and ‌at risk of bursting.

Rescuers were forced to suspend their search for survivors, while residents who had returned to Rasuwa were told to evacuate their homes. Many were seen fleeing up the hillsides to escape a possible surge in the river.

In a video on YouTube, Jaggi Vasudev, known as Sadhguru, a spiritual leader who founded the nonprofit Isha Foundation, told followers at the foundation’s camp at Saga in Tibet , China, that 80 members of an Isha group returning from Kailash Mansarovar, a high-altitude site in ‌Tibet revered by Hindus and Buddhists, were missing, including nine British people.

Among them was Neetu Goyal Tiwari, 51. Her brother Naresh Goyal told the BBC that completing the pilgrimage was “her dream”. Neetu’s nephew, Anmol Goyal, said she had been travelling with a friend, and that her last known location was at the immigration centre on the Tibet-Nepal border. He said she had been added to the Nepalese government’s official list of missing persons.

The family have been desperately phoning contacts in Nepal in an attempt to find her, though they increasingly believe her to still be in China. As many of them are based in India, it is difficult for them to obtain visas to search for her. Goyal said her husband and daughter remained in the UK for now.

“We’re not sure what the next second holds and what we should do from our end, because we’re trying to reach everyone we can,” he said. “She was a very fun-loving woman [and] really had a great heart. I really hope she comes back soon.”

The Telegraph reported that an NHS psychiatrist, Pravin Atmakur, 54, was leading a group of 77 pilgrims on Isha Foundation’s journey to Mount Kailash. The group’s last-known location was an immigration centre in Timure, in the mudslide’s direct path. His wife, Manjula Atmakur, who arrived in Kathmandu to search for him on Friday, told the newspaper she was disappointed by the British government’s response to the disaster.

Fishtail Tours and Travels confirmed Leena Bector, 53, from Slough, was among 27 travellers in its group who were unaccounted for.

Her husband, Bhupesh Bector, told the Times he was booking the next flight to Kathmandu after the Home Office had failed to confirm whether Leena was on its missing persons list. “Even if they find her today or tomorrow, I need to be there,” he said. “She must be in trauma.” Also missing are an A-level student from Surrey, Spandan Sahu, 18, and his father, Santosh Sahu, 46, the chief executive of the UK pharmaceutical technology company Charac; Spandan’s mother, Surabhi Manmath Padhy, 44; and sister Syna Kumari Sahu, 13.

Mahadev Semwal, a friend of Sahu’s for about 15 years, said: “I had WhatsApp communication with him on Monday: they were going to Nepal then Manasarovar in Tibet.

“When I heard on Wednesday about the flooding, I lost contact with him – when I am trying to message him it is getting delivered but not read.

“Our heart says they are safe somewhere. It’s possible because the communication is jammed.

“But when you see the videos, it is unbelievable. It feels so bad.”

Also confirmed missing was Sarada Simkhada, a senior nurse from Dartford, Kent, who left for Nepal last Saturday on a religious journey. Deepesh Patel told the Press Association that his parents, Bipin Patel, 66, and Mala Patel, 60, from Coventry, were missing after flying to Nepal on 22 August for a pilgrimage. His brother Anant Patel told Sky News he was “shocked” at the lack of information on their whereabouts.

Vikram Kolagatla, from London, told the BBC he had not heard from his wife, Geetha Reddy. Reddy, who has two daughters aged 12 and 14, had been in Hotel Kailash in Rasuwagadh when the flooding hit.

“We’re not sure what to do. I have two little girls, and their schools are starting next week,” Kolagatla added.

Tatjana Phillips, from Folkestone in Kent, told the BBC she had not been able to contact her sister, Julija Jakovicka, who was attending a yoga and meditation retreat near the Nepal-Tibet border when flash flooding hit.

Tanay Ranjan told the BBC he had not heard from his older brother Ankit Ranjan, 39, or sister-in-law, Ankita Chandra, 35, who had gone on a pilgrimage.

Ranjan added: “We don’t know if they crossed the border … We don’t have a clue where they are. We are very much devastated.”

The tour operator Alpine Eco Trek said it had been unable to make contact with a party of 12 Britons aged 13 to 65 who had booked a tour to Mount Kailash in Tibet, and were in the vicinity when the flash floods hit.

Sunil Amin, from Croydon in south London, shared with the Daily Mail the “horrible, horrible feeling” of repeatedly trying to phone his wife, Hema Amin, 63, who was on a pilgrimage with Alpine Eco Trek from Nepal to Tibet with her sister. “I’m devastated,” he said.

The Trekkers’ Society, which organises tours across Nepal, Tibet and Bhutan, said nine UK nationals on a pilgrimage had gone missing. The organisation confirmed that four men and boys aged between 14 and 50 and five women aged 40 to 53 were unaccounted for.

Himalayan Glacier US said it had lost contact with a group of 47 guests and staff, including two Britons, who were also on a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash, regarded as the spiritual home of the Hindu god Shiva.

The tour operator Kailash Journeys confirmed it had not been able to account for seven UK nationals – five women and two men aged between 18 and 55 – who were travelling with it. Leaf Holidays, which runs Himalayan treks and expeditions from Kathmandu, wrote in a Facebook post that its group of 55 travellers remained missing, including four British citizens, Tara and Babar Gurung and Thaneswar and Tejkumari Gurung, who have not been heard from since Tuesday.

Twelve of the missing British citizens were on a tour to Mount Kailash led by Nabhi Nandan Das, a 64-year-old Hindu priest who works at the Sanatan Mandir and community centre in Surrey, the Telegraph reported. He is understood to have been leading 11 Britons on a tour that was due to visit Kailash and Lake Mansarovar, two Hindu holy sites in Tibet.

Pramod Poudel, who runs a Nepalese street food company in Sussex, told the Daily Mail his wife, Sumitra, mother, Tulisa, brother Pradip and uncle Madav were all missing. His father, Purusottam, has been found alive.

The Non-Resident Nepali Association in the UK launched an emergency fundraising appeal on Thursday and more than £12,000 has been raised.

Rajendra Pudasaini, a nurse in Essex who is president of the Non-Resident Nepali Association UK, said Nepal was witnessing an “irreplaceable loss” and Nepal was “paying the price for global warming”.

Pudasaini told BBC Radio 4 Today’s programme that many of his family members were missing. “My godson, we found the body yesterday morning, you know, he (was) just buried under the mud at his house, and yes, lots of other dead bodies being found.”

He added: “It’s a very difficult situation to describe, actually.”

Risk of fresh flooding had forced rescue teams to withdraw as residents rushed up hills to escape possible river surge

Nepal-Tibet flash flood – latest updates

Visual guide: how the deadly flooding unfolded

Tell us: have you been affected by the flash floods?

Rescuers searching for survivors of deadly flash floods on the Nepal-Tibet border have resumed their efforts after suspending operations when a debris dam burst its bank on Friday, increasing the risk of fresh flooding.

Residents in Nepal’s Rasuwa district, on the border with Tibet, were seen rushing up hillsides ⁠on Friday to escape a possible surge in the river, ⁠according to witnesses. Fears of another flood came as authorities in Nepal and China said that at least 543 people had been killed in the disaster.

More than 500 foreign citizens were among 826 people missing in Nepal , police and tourism ⁠officials said, including 177 from India, 90 from the US, 34 from Australia, 33 from Britain and 25 from Canada. Chinese state media said at least 558 were missing on the Tibet side of the border, of whom at least 260 were foreign nationals.

The flood on Wednesday had destroyed power stations, roads and bridges along a route that links Kathmandu with Lhasa in Tibet and is ⁠popular with trekkers and pilgrims.

The Chinese state broadcaster CCTV reported that a lake formed by piles of debris from the mudslide had begun overflowing on Friday, sending water towards the area where rescue teams were headed, and forcing a brief pause in operations.

Rescue efforts in Bidur, the capital of the Nuwakot district in Bagmati province, Nepal, were disrupted on Friday morning as the the Trishuli River began to rise again after the lake near the China border burst its banks.

Rescue workers were moved from the area and people who had tried to return to what remained of their homes were told to evacuate again immediately.

Bidur, once a bustling town on the banks of the Trishuli, now lies in ruins. Most homes were washed away when a tide of mud, rocks and debris surged down the river valley early on Wednesday. Survivors described clinging to buildings and trees as the water rushed over them.

The mangled concrete remains of a bank, a government office and an ATM booth were among the few structures left standing, although they were submerged in mud. Officials said there were still bodies inside the buildings but it was too dangerous to recover them.

Nearby, local people gathered along the muddy road, calling out for lost relatives and trying to dig out what was left of their belongings.

Most areas battered by flash floods remained accessible only by army helicopter. At the Bidur army camp, where much of the rescue effort was being coordinated, rescue and military helicopters flew in and out every five minutes, bringing in dozens of traumatised victims. Many said that in a matter of minutes, the floods had taken their loved ones, their homes and everything they owned.

The international community is scrambling to get aid to flood-stricken parts of Nepal and Tibet.

Nepal has said it does not yet need foreign assistance as the search-and-rescue operation – complicated by the destruction of dozens of bridges and miles of roads across the mountainous region – continues.

“The offer for help is natural,” Lok Bahadur Chhetri, a spokesperson for Nepal’s foreign ministry, said on Friday. “Our security agencies ‌are doing the search and rescue operation. For now we don’t require such help.”

The Kathmandu Post reported that India, China, the US, Britain, Japan, South Korea, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh had asked the government to allow their search-and-rescue teams to assist in the operation.

Dinesh Bhattarai, a former Nepali ⁠ambassador to the UN in Geneva, said the government’s reluctance to ​accept foreign assistance may ​be linked to sensitivities over ​Rasuwa district and its border with China’s Tibet region.

“They may have thought about ​the locational sensitivity ‌of the region and ​decided not to ​accept foreign teams,” Bhattarai told Reuters.

But Chhetri said Nepal’s own rescue teams were handling the operation and the decision to refuse foreign assistance had nothing to do with sensitivities involving China.

Scant information has emerged from Chinese authorities about the scale of the destruction in Tibet, the most tightly controlled part of China even under normal circumstances. Only brief, state-controlled media reports about the floods have been allowed to circulate in China and the authorities have confirmed only three deaths there. Chinese reports have focused on rescue efforts.

In Nepal earlier on Friday, army helicopter rescue teams were working to free about 100 people trapped in a tunnel at a flooded hydropower project.

“Our focus is in search and rescue of people … some people are trapped in the tunnel of Trishuli 3A hydropower project,” said the Nepal army spokesperson, Raja Ram Basnet.

“Two helicopters have been dispatched but it is challenging because it is tough to even locate the entry points of the tunnel. Relief efforts are also under way to provide the rescued people what they need.”

The prime minister’s office said the army was working in challenging conditions and had rescued 350 workers and local people who were trapped in the tunnel.

Rescue teams reported finding bodies hundreds of miles downstream from the disaster zone in the Chitwan district of Nepal, near the Tibetan border. Dozens of injured people were transported to Kathmandu for advanced medical care and more than 100 people were rescued by Nepali army personnel in helicopters.

CCTV said 499 Chinese nationals and 555 foreigners had been transported out of the disaster zone as of Friday.

Scale of devastation emerges in Nepal as reporters reach disaster area, but Chinese state media focus more on rescue efforts

Nepal-Tibet flash flood – latest updates

In the days since an enormous glacier in the Himalayas snapped away from a mountaintop and cascaded into the valley below, the true scale of the devastation caused by the flash floods in Nepal and Tibet is still unfolding.

But the picture is emerging far more quickly in Nepal than in China, where strict controls on the flow of information from one of its most sensitive regions are hampering the public’s understanding of events.

The floods devastated villages along the Himalayan border region that straddles Nepal and the Chinese region of Tibet. On Friday, the official death toll in Nepal rose to 538 people, while in China it was just five, despite the fact that the villages around the Gyirong border crossing are home to several thousand people.

In Nepal, journalists rushed to get as close to the disaster zone as possible to interview survivors and rescue workers. Villagers provided minute-by-minute accounts of what happened when the floods, the exact cause of which is still being studied by scientists, tore through their homes.

In China, state media carried several broadcasts about the floods and dispatched their own journalists to the area, but reports focused on the rescue efforts rather than the scale of the devastation. In one broadcast from a relief centre in Tibet, the journalist did not speak to any of the people sitting behind him.

Tibet, brought under Chinese control in the 1950s, is the most sensitive and tightly controlled region in the country. Sporadic protests, including self-immolations, by Tibetans calling for more autonomy and religious freedom have been cracked down on by the authorities. International journalists cannot visit Tibet apart from on tightly choreographed government tours. Many Tibetans are not allowed passports and have very limited contact with the outside world. Tibetans can be punished for speaking to journalists. Human rights groups have for years criticised Beijing’s policies on Tibetan language and culture, which activists say are under attack.

That makes independent assessments of how the flash floods have affected the Tibetan side of the border difficult.

“Everything about Tibet is seen through the national security prism. And therefore nobody is going to say anything or report anything that has not been cleared from the very top,” said Steve Tsang, the director of the China Institute at Soas University of London.

For anyone on the ground, “you can’t report a higher figure of deaths, even if you have seen more bodies yourself, until the official statement says that the figure has gone up”.

China’s tight controls on information are limiting international coverage of its relief efforts. That may mean China is missing an opportunity to tell its own good news story.

Chinese emergency services, including the People’s Liberation Army, are vastly better resourced than their Nepalese counterparts. Navigating the difficult, mountainous terrain where conditions are still unsafe requires specialised expertise. China has dispatched hundreds of emergency service personnel but there is scant detail on what they are doing. “The Chinese have missed a trick,” Tsang said. But “they don’t have that confidence. Their instinct is control.”

Still, China has been keen to stress that the disaster is a national priority. China’s leader, Xi Jinping, chaired a meeting on Friday to direct rescue work, according to state media. Xi called on the authorities to “make every effort to search for missing people from China and abroad”. He also dispatched his number two, premier Li Qiang, to visit the affected area. According to the state-run Xinhua news agency, Li “emphasised that General Secretary Xi Jinping is deeply concerned about the people in the disaster-stricken areas”.

Hundreds of foreigners were in area to work, take guided treks or make pilgrimages when disaster struck

Nepal-Tibet flash flood – latest updates

Flash floods at the Nepal-Tibet border have killed at least 543 people and more than 1,500 are missing. Hundreds were foreigners in the area to work, take guided treks or make pilgrimages.

Thousands have been rescued, with some of the injured taken to hospitals in Nepal’s capital, Kathmandu. The number of missing may vary because of progress in the ongoing rescue efforts and differences in how data has been collected and verified among agencies.

Here is how different countries have been affected.

Nepal

Nepal’s disaster management authority said on Friday the death toll in that country had risen to 538, with 977 people missing. The authority said 3,253 people had been rescued by helicopter, and more than 150 of the injured were taken to hospitals in Kathmandu and the districts of Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading.

Local reports cited the National Emergency Operation Centre as saying on Thursday that the missing included 113 Nepali tourists, 85 personnel from the army and police, 161 residents from the Rasuwa district and one from the Nuwakot district.

China

State media reported on Friday that at least five people had died and 558 were missing in Gyirong County, Tibet. The state broadcaster CCTV reported that 260 of the 558 missing people were foreigners. In addition, nearly 100 Chinese citizens were missing on the Nepal side, China’s foreign ministry said.

India

India’s foreign ministry said 288 Indian nationals remained uncontactable, including 73 people who were working on a power project. Nepali officials said many Indian tourists were on pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet, a sacred site for Hindus.

US

The US state department said 90 of its citizens were unaccounted for in China and Nepal, but that it was not aware of any US deaths. Three Americans have been rescued.

Malaysia

Officials said 51 Malaysians were missing.

Ukraine

Ukraine’s foreign ministry said 55 Ukrainians were missing. The number includes two tourist groups, of 47 and seven people respectively, in addition to one Ukrainian woman travelling with a foreign tour group.

Australia

The Australian government said 39 Australians were missing.

Britain

Officials said 33 of the missing were from Britain.

Canada

The Nepal tourism board (NTB) said 25 of the missing were from Canada .

South Korea

South Korean government officials said nine citizens working on the construction of a hydropower plant in Nepal were missing.

Singapore

Eight Singaporeans were missing, according to the NTB.

Germany

The NTB said eight tourists from Germany were missing.

Russia

The Russian embassy in Nepal said eight of its citizens were missing.

South Africa

The NTB said six South Africans were missing.

Latvia

The NTB said six tourists from Latvia were missing.

Japan

Japanese media said five Japanese tourists were missing, made up of a couple and their children.

New Zealand

Five people from New Zealand were missing, the NTB said.

France

The NTB said four French citizens were missing.

Belgium

The NTB said three people from Belgium were missing.

Spain

The NTB said three visitors from Spain were missing.

Others

The NTB said two people each from Italy, Kazakhstan, Portugal, Ireland and the Netherlands were missing. It said 10 others – one each from Belarus, Finland, Hungary, Israel, Lithuania, the Philippines, Bulgaria, Switzerland, Serbia and Sweden – were also missing.

stories.body:
Roadmap for increasing department’s share of GDP will be deferred until next year’s review

The chancellor will delay setting out when the UK will meet the target of allocating 3% of GDP on defence until next year’s spending review, the Treasury has confirmed.

John Healey resigned as defence secretary in June under Keir Starmer’s leadership, accusing the prime minister of being “unable” and the Treasury “unwilling” to “commit the resources that the nation needs to defend the country”.

However, since succeeding Rachel Reeves following Andy Burnham’s arrival at No 10, Healey has declined to set a date for meeting the 3% target, which he had previously insisted should be hit by 2030.

Treasury sources confirmed that instead, the focus in Healey’s first budget on 28 October, would be fully funding the defence investment plan.

The three-year DIP was one of Starmer’s final announcements – but about £1.2bn a year was left unaccounted for, with Healey’s predecessor Reeves suggesting the money would have to be found through cuts in other Whitehall departments.

The Treasury confirmed on Friday that there would be no further detail about the timeline in the budget. A spending review is expected to be held next year but no date has yet been set.

A government spokesperson said: “The first duty of government is to keep its citizens safe. The prime minister and chancellor are committed to fully funding the defence investment plan. At the spending review we will set out a pathway to meet our Nato commitment of 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035 and will set a target date to hit 3% on that path.”

Defence spending is on track to reach 2.7% of GDP by 2030, funded partly by Starmer’s decision to cut the UK’s aid spending.

Healey had previously said that this figure should rise to 3% urgently, given the growing global conflicts and security risks. He wrote in his resignation letter to Starmer in June : “As we have regularly discussed, I am certain that a headmark date for 3% of GDP on defence in 2030 is what Britain must set.” So far, the prime minister, Burnham, has refused to commit to the 3% target.

In an interview with Sky News on Friday, Healey said fiscal discipline was the “first priority” for any chancellor.

The chancellor will fly to North Carolina this weekend for a meeting of G20 finance ministers, chaired by the US Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent.

Healey and his colleagues will discuss the prospects for global growth, against the backdrop of continued high energy prices, volatile government bond markets and the US-Canada trade war.

stories.body:
Flash floods have killed at least 469 people while homes and infrastructure have been swept away

Nepal-Tibet flash flood – latest updates

What caused the flash flood in Nepal and Tibet?

The international community was scrambling to get aid into flood-stricken parts of Nepal and Tibet on Thursday as authorities warned that a lake ⁠formed at the ⁠site ⁠where the ​deadly torrents occurred ⁠was rising and ⁠at risk ​of ‌bursting.

The catastrophic flash floods that hit Nepal and Tibet on Wednesday, thundering down valleys and obliterating entire villages, killed at least 469 people and left more than 1,300 missing.

Efforts to locate those unaccounted for – including hundreds of tourists from India, the US, Britain, Australia and Canada – have been complicated by the destruction of dozens of bridges and 25 miles (40km) of roads in the mountainous region, which is popular with trekkers and pilgrims.

Nepali army helicopter rescue teams were working on Friday to rescue about 100 people trapped inside a tunnel at a hydropower project swamped by the devastating flood.

“Our focus is in search and rescue of people … some people are trapped in the tunnel of Trishuli 3A hydropower project,” said Nepal army spokesman Raja Ram Basnet.

“Two helicopters have been dispatched but it is challenging because it is tough to even locate the entry points of the tunnel. Relief efforts are also under way to provide the rescued people what they need.”

The prime minister’s office said the army was working in tough conditions and had already rescued 350 workers and local people who were trapped in the tunnel amid the risky conditions.

Rescue teams reported finding bodies hundreds of miles downstream from the disaster zone in the Chitwan district of Nepal, near the border with India. Dozens of injured people were transported to Kathmandu for advanced medical care and more than 100 people were rescued by Nepali army personnel in helicopters.

Videos from Wednesday showed a massive wall of water crashing down on the border as people tried to flee. The power, volume and speed of the floods gave little time for escape.

Trucks were overturned and houses, roads ⁠and power plants were swept away in Nepal, while ​officials in Tibet said they feared “major casualties” after a mudslide hit a border crossing.

Tom Fletcher, the UN’s humanitarian chief, described the flood as “horrifying”. He said emergency teams had been mobilised and an initial $2m (£1.5m) of disaster funds allocated to cover emergency medical care, shelter and water.

Nepal’s disaster authority warned of continuing danger on Thursday, appealing to residents and rescuers to stay away from a swelling lake that had formed at the flood site. Chinese authorities said a barrier lake at the confluence of the Tsogyal and Purupqiangzangbu rivers was overflowing and could burst.

Girilal Budhathoki, 36, who lives in the Rasuwa district of Nepal’s Bagmati province, said the flood waters swept away his wife and four children while he was away from the family home.

“A huge surge of water came,” he said. “Everything turned completely black, and I couldn’t understand what was happening. Suddenly, something heavy crushed me and I fell down.”

Budhathoki realised what had happened only when he returned to the place where his house had stood. “I searched desperately for my wife and children but I couldn’t find them,” he said. “They didn’t make it out. My wife was swept away too. I am all alone now.”

Kamal Kharel, who works at a hydropower plant in Chilime, also in Rasuwa district, was in the office when the floods hit. “The whole place shook as if there had been a huge earthquake,” he said. “But when I went outside, I saw everything a storm and raging water.”

Kharel and some of his colleagues managed to climb a hill, where they stayed until they were rescued by the army on Thursday morning. “I had never seen waves crashing that high. You only see waves like that in the sea.”

People from the hard-hit districts of Nuwakot and Dhading, in Bagmati province, were seen gathering outside an army training centre – the base for helicopter rescue operations – seeking information about missing family members.

Police were recording the names of the missing outside the barracks gate. Mobile phone torches were their only source of light as the area remained without electricity because of damaged hydroelectric infrastructure.

The village of Soley, in Nuwakot, which had about 25 homes, was almost wiped out, according to Nirajan Paudyal, a Kathmandu-based journalist whose parents and other relatives lived there. Desperate for information, he had travelled to the area on Thursday for news of his family. “There is no update till now,” he said. “I fear there won’t be any update.”

More than 500 foreigners were among 826 people missing in Nepal, police and tourism ⁠officials said. Among those unaccounted for were 177 from India, 90 from the US, 34 from Australia, 33 from Britain and 25 from Canada.

Chinese state media said at least 558 were missing on the Tibet side of the border, of whom at least 260 were foreign nationals.

Many of the victims were on a pilgrimage to Kailash Mansarovar, a high-altitude site in ‌Tibet revered by Hindus and Buddhists among others.

Early reports from Nepali ​officials suggested an earthquake could have caused the lower part of a glacier to collapse and trigger ‌the floods. But the US Geological Survey later said what was initially reported ‌as a 4.4-magnitude earthquake was a seismic shock generated by glacial rock and ice collapsing, causing the flood of debris. “No earthquake had occurred,” it said.

Srijana Gurung, the acting Nepal director for the international NGO Plan International, said communities across the Himalayan country were facing “climate shock after shock” with hardly any time to recover.

“Floods and landslides have always happened in Nepal but the climate crisis is making them far more frequent and intense,” she said. “The priority now must be reaching those affected, supporting families searching for loved ones and ensuring vulnerable communities have the assistance they need.”

Gurung said children and families who had lost their homes and livelihoods would be in urgent need of medical help, food, shelter and hygiene kits. “There is also a risk of waterborne disease as access to clean water and sanitation is likely to have been damaged,” she said.

Scant information emerged from Chinese authorities about the scale of the destruction. Tibet is the most tightly controlled part of China even under normal circumstances. Foreign journalists cannot visit the region unless they are part of a government-controlled tour and the authorities have cracked down harshly on calls for greater autonomy from the Tibetan people. Tibetans have almost no contact with the international media because of fears of retribution.

Only brief, state-controlled media reports about the floods have been allowed to circulate in China and the authorities have confirmed only three deaths. Chinese reports have focused on rescue efforts.

Maya Wang, the deputy Asia director at Human Rights Watch, wrote on X: “The floods raise questions about whether Chinese authorities could’ve done more to reduce disaster risks, given longstanding concerns from Tibetan diaspora groups and experts about rapid, state-led development in areas where Tibetans have little say.”

She called on Beijing to “allow Tibetans access to information and international researchers and journalists unfettered access to the region, and conduct a rigorous investigation into the disaster”.

stories.body:
Unusual heat this year may have melted ice and thawed bonds that hold glaciers in place – leading to catastrophe

Nepal-Tibet flash flood – latest updates

What caused the flash flood in Nepal and Tibet?

The devastating flash flood that has ripped through the border communities of Nepal and Tibet has heightened fears that the climate crisis is destabilising the geology of mountain and polar regions, threatening millions of people.

Satellite imagery suggests a glacier collapse high in the Himalayas was the primary cause of the deadly torrent of mud, water and ice that tore along the Bhotekoshi River on Wednesday. It swept away buildings and roads and left at least 360 dead and 1,400 missing.

A magnitude 4.4 earthquake was initially blamed for the collapse. However, it is now thought to have been caused by the huge wall of ice that crashed down on to the north slope of Langtang Lirung, a 7,000-metre (23,000ft) mountain, the impact of which registered a magnitude of 5.2.

“Additional analysis of long-period seismic waves indicates that the seismic energy was instead generated by a glacial collapse and debris flow,” the US Geological Survey said .

The ice-rock avalanche pushed boulders and other debris into the Lhende Khola River, a tributary of the Bhotekoshi River. Water levels in rivers downstream rose by between 7 and 9 metres within 30 minutes, according to the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development, an intergovernmental scientific institution.

Scientists are still examining the precise mechanics of the Himalayan disaster, but many observe that glaciers and permafrost around the world are being weakened by global heating, caused by the burning of gas, oil and coal.

The detachment of a chunk of the glacier wall came amid unusual heat that was likely to have melted the ice that bound the splintered bedrock together.

Two days before the collapse, the ground temperature hit its highest point in the last two years, according to Dr Hamish Pritchard, a glaciologist with the British Antarctic Survey, whose team had sensors 6 miles (10km) away from the site.

“These high temperatures would have weakened the snowpack, filled crevasses with water and thawed the bonds between ice and rock that hold these glaciers in place,” he told the Science Media Centre.

A series of intense heatwaves has hit the region since early this year and affected countries around the world. Another factor here was the monsoon season, which saturated the soil and swelled rivers.

Disasters like this were foretold. In 2023 the UN’s top scientific advisory body warned that previously ice-bound landmasses – from permafrost tundra to mountain glaciers – would become increasingly unstable as temperatures rose.

“Every increment of warming will multiply and intensify future hazards from cryosphere regions,” observed the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change in its sixth synthesis report. “Floods, landslides and freshwater shortages from glacier retreat and snow loss pose a serious threat to mountain regions across the world.”

Average global temperatures are nudging closer to 1.5C above preindustrial levels. Even faster warming is occurring in alpine and polar regions because the loss of snow and ice is removing the thermal insulation of the land.

Dr Richard Waller, a senior lecturer in physical geography at Keele University, said: “The progressive loss of snow and glacier ice results in the surface being less reflective, so it absorbs more solar energy and heats up. In combination with atmospheric warming, this is leading to the melting of mountain permafrost.

“Think of the high mountains like this as shattered bedrock glued together by ice-filled joints. As the permafrost and the ice-filled joints melt, then there’s the potential for these types of catastrophic failure.”

The thaw is altering the shape, colour and solidity of the landscape, creating or expanding glacial meltwater lakes and, in the long term, threatening the origin of many rivers and the drinking supplies of populations downstream. In many parts of Asia, hundreds of millions of people depend on the rivers such as the Ganges and the Brahmaputra that descend from the glaciers.

Scientists have high confidence that glacier retreat is caused by human-driven global heating. This has caused glacier collapses from the Alps to the Andes. In the Langtang catchment area in Nepal, glacier loss rates have increased more than fourfold since 1964, a study has shown .

This has contributed to a loss of life on multiple occasions. A smaller flood hit the Bhotekoshi River in July 2025 and in 2015, the Langtang Lirung mountain was hit by an earthquake-induced avalanche that destroyed Langtang village.

As emergency services look for bodies and humanitarian relief groups mobilise for survivors, others are asking where next. Waller said any high mountain areas with glaciers and permafrost could be vulnerable, including the European Alps, Caucasus, Himalayas, Andes and beyond.

As glacier weakening accelerates, Pritchard called for greater disaster preparedness. “More avalanches and more floods are inevitable, particularly as lakes grow in front of the retreating glaciers,” he said. “Early warning systems are urgently needed to protect the people living in these valleys.”

stories.title: Ex-council chief investigated in DUP mayor clothing probe
stories.summary: Anne Donaghy is one of three people referred to prosecutors for consideration over alleged misconduct in public office.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Anne Donaghy pictured outside court earlier this week

Published 28 August 2026, 00:04 BST

An ex-council chief executive is a subject in a police investigation into a former Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) mayor's clothing expenses.

Anne Donaghy is one of three people referred to prosecutors for consideration over alleged misconduct in public office at Mid and East Antrim Borough Council.

It is the latest case surrounding its handling of Freedom of Information (FoI) legislation after Donaghy was convicted on Wednesday of two charges over the deletion of an email to former DUP leader Arlene Foster.

Donaghy's solicitor told BBC News NI the allegations would be "met with the same robustness as this week's proceedings which are now under appeal".

The Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) confirmed a file has been submitted to the Public Prosecution Service (PPS) for consideration.

Police said the investigation was in respect of two women aged 56 and 42, and a 57-year-old man.

None of the three are the former DUP mayor whose expenses were examined.

DUP leader Gavin Robinson said that "as far as I'm aware there are no issues that pertain to my colleagues or my party".

"These are issues for Ms Donaghy to deal with," he told the BBC Ulster's Good Morning Ulster programme .

Expenses cheque

The case centres on questions over clothing expenses claimed by Audrey Wales, 80, who was mayor between 2016 and 2017.

The Ballymena councillor spent more than £2,300, but the council did not disclose the full cost when asked for details in an FoI request.

Instead its response in 2019 said Wales had spent just £190.

The entire bill was only revealed in a second FoI in 2022.

In a statement in 2022, Wales said she had sent a cheque in 2019 reimbursing the council for most of the spending to stop "electorally motivated questions".

The cheque was received by Donaghy, but was never cashed.

Wales, who sent a second cheque in 2021 upon learning the first had not been processed, said that "at all times" she acted in line with "guidance from council officials".

The council in 2022 commissioned a Belfast-based firm to conduct an investigation.

It found the council's FoI response involved "a deliberate manipulation", according to a copy leaked to the Belfast Telegraph. , external

Donaghy has previously denied being involved in discussions about the FOI and said an email she sent referring to the cheque showed that she intended to cash it.

When asked at the time whether it was examining the case, the PSNI said detectives were continuing to "investigate suspected offences of misconduct in public office and under the Freedom of Information Act 2000".

In an update, a PSNI spokesperson told BBC News NI: "A file was submitted to the PPS in January 2025 concerning this investigation in respect of two females aged 56 and 42, and a 57-year-old man."

It is understood the investigation file relates to alleged offences including misconduct in a public office.

The PPS does not comment on any evidence in a file while it remains under consideration.

The case emerges after Donaghy was on Wednesday convicted of two charges connected to deleting or attempting to delete an email to prevent disclosure under the Freedom of Information Act.

The 56-year-old, of Clonmore Road, Dungannon, was fined £1,500. She was cleared of a third charge of trying to have an email deleted.

'Vehemently contest'

On Wednesday Donaghy's solicitor said she "maintains her innocence" and would "vehemently contest" the findings.

In a further statement on the clothing expenses case, her solicitor said: "These are allegations of some considerable vintage stretching back a number of years.

"If they ever materialise into anything then they will be met with the same robustness as this week's proceedings which are now under appeal."

Mid and East Antrim Borough Council has said it will "carefully consider the outcome and any implications arising" from this week's trial.

It added the council is "committed to the highest standards of governance, transparency and information management".

The Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) has urged public bodies to ensure they have proper arrangements to "protect" official records.

In a statement an ICO spokesperson said: "Public authorities must have robust records management practices in place and take appropriate steps to preserve information that is subject to a request under Freedom of Information legislation."

stories.title: South of France holiday scuppers Davey's blood donation
stories.summary: The Lib Dem leader was unable to give blood due to visiting an area where there is the risk of mosquito-borne viruses.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Ed Davey posing in front of adverts for blood donation at Brixton underground station before trying to donate at the nearby NHS Blood Donor Centre

Published 7 hours ago

A summer holiday to the south of France scuppered Sir Ed Davey's attempt to give blood to the NHS.

The Liberal Democrat leader had been poised to donate at the Brixton Donor Centre but, after filling out paperwork, was told he could not go ahead due to his recent trip to the Charente region.

The NHS says those returning from certain parts of France between May and November should wait four weeks before donating due to the risk of mosquito-borne viruses.

A Liberal Democrat spokesperson said Sir Ed would return to give blood once the 28 days had passed.

His visit to the south London centre was part of a campaign to promote blood donations to "beat the winter crisis" in the NHS.

NHS Blood Donation says it needs over 140,000 people to donate blood for the first time this year to meet demand. Blood has a shelf life of 35 days, so stocks need constant replenishing.

Earlier this year, the NHS warned it faced "a significant shortfall in blood stocks with hot weather, holidays and high demand all significantly impacting supplies".

Gerry Gogarth, director of blood and plasma supply at NHS Blood and Transplant said: "We urgently need anyone eligible to donate to book an appointment as soon as they can."

Anyone wishing to donate blood can sign up on the NHS Blood Donation website, , external external or use the app to register and book an appointment.

There are restrictions on who can donate blood including limits on those who have recently travelled to particular areas.

In Sir Ed's case, the risk of exposure to ChikV and Dengue virus in parts of France prevented him from donating.

The French regions covered by the restriction are Bouches-du-Rhône, Charente, Dordogne, Hautes-Pyrénées, Haute-Garonne, Pyrénées-Orientales, Var, Gard, Hérault, Isere, Alpes-Maritimes, Vaucluse or Corsica.

A Lib Dem spokesperson said: "Ed unfortunately could not give blood today due to recent changes to rules regarding blood donations after travelling to certain destinations.

"Ed went to the Charente region in France on holiday which poses an infection risk due to mosquito prevalence, he will have to wait 28 days after returning home in order to give blood. He'll be back."
